name: Isaac Newton
info: Isaac Newton (1643–1727) was an English mathematician, physicist and polymath whose Principia of 1687 set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation, and who also worked on optics and calculus and served as Master of the Royal Mint.

facts.born: 25 December 1642 by the Julian calendar then in use in England (4 January 1643 New Style) at Woolsthorpe Manor, Woolsthorpe-by-Colsterworth, Lincolnshire; son of Isaac Newton, who had died three months before, and Hannah Ayscough
facts.died: 20 March 1727 (31 March New Style) in London, in his sleep, aged 84; buried in the nave of Westminster Abbey after a state funeral
facts.role: Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge (from 1667); Lucasian Professor of Mathematics (from 1669); Fellow of the Royal Society (1672) and its president (1703–1727); Member of Parliament for the University of Cambridge (1689–1690, 1701–1702); Warden (1696–1699) and Master (1699–1727) of the Royal Mint; knighted 1705
facts.known: the laws of motion and universal gravitation; the Principia (1687); infinitesimal calculus, for which he shares credit with Leibniz; his theory of colour and Opticks (1704); the first reflecting telescope; the recoinage and the prosecution of counterfeiters at the Royal Mint

t: Born after his father's death at a Lincolnshire manor, Newton developed his theories on calculus, optics and the law of gravitation at home in the two years after 1665, when Cambridge closed against the plague.

The Principia of 1687 stated three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, which formed the dominant scientific viewpoint for centuries until it was superseded by the theory of relativity.

He spent his last three decades in London at the Royal Mint and the Royal Society, fell out with Hooke, Leibniz and Flamsteed, and kept his rejection of the Trinity and most of his alchemy unpublished.
dyk: Newton's library contained 1,752 books that could be identified, of which 477 were on theology and 169 on alchemy; books related to his famous scientific work made up slightly less than 12% of the collection.
ev: Born at Woolsthorpe Manor, Lincolnshire, on Christmas Day 1642 by the Julian calendar then in use in England, three months after his father's death
Admitted to Trinity College at the University of Cambridge, where he starts as a subsizar
Takes his BA; the university closes against the Great Plague, and over the next two years at Woolsthorpe he develops theories on calculus, optics and gravitation
Succeeds Isaac Barrow as Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at the age of 26
The Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica is published with encouragement and financial help from Edmond Halley
Moves to London as Warden of the Mint and takes charge of England's great recoining
Publishes Opticks, a year after becoming president of the Royal Society
Dies in his sleep in London, aged 84, and is buried in Westminster Abbey after a state funeral

sections.early:
Isaac Newton was born on Christmas Day, 25 December 1642 by the Julian calendar then in use in England (4 January 1643 New Style), at Woolsthorpe Manor in Woolsthorpe-by-Colsterworth, a hamlet in Lincolnshire. His father, also named Isaac Newton, had died three months before. Born prematurely, he was a small child. When he was three his mother, Hannah Ayscough, remarried and went to live with her new husband, the Reverend Barnabas Smith, leaving him in the care of his maternal grandmother, Margery Ayscough. He disliked his stepfather: a list of sins committed up to the age of 19 includes "Threatening my father and mother Smith to burn them and the house over them."

From about the age of twelve until he was seventeen he was educated at The King's School in Grantham. By October 1659 his mother, widowed a second time, had removed him and tried to make him a farmer, an occupation he hated; the school's master, Henry Stokes, and his uncle, the Reverend William Ayscough, persuaded her to send him back. He became the top-ranked student, distinguishing himself mainly by building sundials and models of windmills.

In June 1661 he was admitted to Trinity College, Cambridge, on his uncle's recommendation. He started as a subsizar, paying his way by valet duties until he was awarded a scholarship in 1664. Cambridge's teachings were based on Aristotle, whom he read along with more modern philosophers. In 1665 he discovered the generalised binomial theorem and began to develop the mathematical theory that later became calculus.
sections.rise:
Soon after Newton obtained his BA in August 1665, the university closed temporarily as a precaution against the Great Plague. He had been undistinguished as a student, but the next two years at his home in Woolsthorpe saw the development of his theories on calculus, optics and the law of gravitation. In 1666 he observed that a prism refracts different colours by different angles and concluded that colour is a property intrinsic to light.

He returned to Cambridge in April 1667 and in October was elected a fellow of Trinity. In 1669, one year after receiving his MA, he succeeded Isaac Barrow as Lucasian Professor of Mathematics, at the age of 26. Fellows were required to take holy orders; King Charles II accepted his argument that the chair should exempt him, and in 1675 he received a government dispensation. As a teacher he was less effective: his classes were almost always empty.

In late 1668 he produced the first known functional reflecting telescope, about eight inches long, grinding the mirror himself. The Royal Society asked for a demonstration in 1671 and elected him a Fellow in 1672, the year of his paper on white light and colours. When Robert Hooke criticised some of his ideas he was so offended that he withdrew from public debate. Exchanges with Hooke in 1679–80 nevertheless stimulated him to prove that the elliptical form of planetary orbits would result from a centripetal force inversely proportional to the square of the radius vector, a result he shared with Edmond Halley and the Royal Society in the tract De motu corporum in gyrum in 1684.
sections.deeds:
The Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica was published on 5 July 1687 with encouragement and financial help from Halley. In it Newton stated three universal laws of motion and formulated the law of universal gravitation. From his mathematical description of gravity he derived Kepler's laws of planetary motion and accounted for tides, the trajectories of comets and the precession of the equinoxes, demonstrating that the motion of objects on Earth and of celestial bodies could be accounted for by the same principles. With the book he became internationally recognised.

His work on calculus, usually referred to as fluxions, began in 1664; the historian of science A. Rupert Hall writes that he was master of its essential techniques by the end of 1666, almost exactly nine years before Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, with whom he is now credited with developing it independently. He also generalised the binomial theorem and classified cubic plane curves. Opticks, published in 1704, collected his work on light, which he argued is composed of particles or corpuscles.

In 1696 he moved to London as Warden of the Mint, and in 1699 he became its Master. The posts were intended as sinecures, but he took charge of the great recoining, estimated that 20 per cent of the coins taken in were counterfeit, conducted more than 100 cross-examinations and successfully prosecuted 28 coiners; the counterfeiter William Chaloner was hanged in 1699. He was made president of the Royal Society in 1703 and was knighted by Queen Anne in April 1705.
sections.opponents:
Newton could be fiercely competitive and on occasion held grudges against his intellectual rivals. He and Robert Hooke disputed over optical discoveries in the 1670s; some historians read his remark to Hooke in February 1675, "If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants", as an oblique attack rather than, or as well as, a statement of modesty. At the Royal Society he made an enemy of John Flamsteed, the Astronomer Royal, by prematurely publishing Flamsteed's Historia Coelestis Britannica, which he had used in his studies.

The dispute with Leibniz over priority in calculus was bitter. Nicolas Fatio de Duillier accused Leibniz of plagiarism from 1699 and John Keill did so in 1708; in 1711 a Royal Society study proclaimed Newton the true discoverer and labelled Leibniz a fraud, and it was later found that Newton himself had written its concluding remarks on Leibniz. The controversy marred the lives of both men until Leibniz's death in 1716.

Newton was criticised for introducing "occult agencies" into science by postulating an invisible force able to act over vast distances; in the second edition of the Principia (1713) he answered that it was improper to frame hypotheses not implied by the phenomena: "Hypotheses non fingo". Privately he rejected the doctrine of the Trinity; the historian Stephen Snobelen calls him a heretic who "never made a public declaration of his private faith". In 1693 he suffered a nervous breakdown and sent wild accusatory letters to his friends Samuel Pepys and John Locke.
sections.last:
Newton spent the last three decades of his life in London. He retired from his Cambridge duties in 1701 and remained Master of the Mint and president of the Royal Society until his death. At the Mint he reduced the standard deviation of the weight of guineas from 1.3 grains to 0.75 grains. A report he wrote on 21 September 1717 led to a royal proclamation of 22 December forbidding the exchange of gold guineas for more than 21 silver shillings, which inadvertently moved Britain from the silver standard to its first gold standard; whether he intended this is a matter of debate.

He was at times an active investor, including in the South Sea Company, and lost at least £10,000, and plausibly more than £20,000, when it collapsed around 1720; already rich, he still died with an estate valued at around £30,000. He never married; his half-niece Catherine Barton served as his hostess at his house on Jermyn Street.

He died in his sleep in London on 20 March 1727 (31 March New Style), aged 84. He was given a state funeral, the first in England for someone recognised primarily for intellectual achievement; his body lay in state in Westminster Abbey for eight days before burial in the nave, and he was the first scientist buried in the abbey. A bachelor, he had divested much of his estate to relatives in his last years and died intestate; his papers went to John Conduitt and Catherine Barton. His hair was later found to contain mercury, probably from his alchemical pursuits.
sections.legacy:
Newton's laws of motion and universal gravitation formed the dominant scientific viewpoint for centuries until superseded by the theory of relativity. Philosophers and historians of the Enlightenment hold that the publication of the Principia was a turning point in the Scientific Revolution and started the Enlightenment: his conception of a universe based on natural and rationally understandable laws became one of the seeds of Enlightenment ideology.

Alexander Pope wrote the epitaph "God said, Let Newton be! and all was light", though it was not allowed on his monument at Westminster; Joseph-Louis Lagrange called the Principia "the greatest production of the human mind". A 1999 poll of 100 leading physicists voted Einstein the "greatest physicist ever" with Newton the runner-up, while a parallel survey of rank-and-file physicists ranked Newton the greatest.

Of an estimated ten million words in his papers, about one million deal with alchemy, and his theological notebooks have been available for public examination only since 1972. The papers were sold at Sotheby's in 1936; John Maynard Keynes reassembled an estimated half of the alchemical papers and donated his collection to Cambridge University in 1946. The Chronology of Ancient Kingdoms Amended was published posthumously in 1728. Newton often told the story that the fall of an apple inspired his theory of gravitation. Of himself he wrote that he seemed "only like a boy playing on the sea-shore" while "the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me".

summary: Isaac Newton (1643–1727), born at Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire, became Lucasian Professor at Cambridge at 26 and in the Principia of 1687 stated the laws of motion and universal gravitation. He also worked on calculus and optics, ran the Royal Mint and presided over the Royal Society, and left unpublished writings on theology and alchemy.

notes: Dates: the article's lead gives 4 January 1643 [O.S. 25 December 1642] – 31 March 1727 [O.S. 20 March 1726]; start 1643 and end 1727 follow the New Style dates given first. The Death section says '20 March 1727 (NS 31 March 1727)' while the lead and the monument give the Old Style death year as 1726 (the Old Style year began in March); the sections use 20 March 1727 as the Death section does. The first event is filed under 1643 but says Christmas Day 1642 by the Julian calendar.

The dispensation from holy orders: the article says both that Charles II accepted his argument (in the 1669 passage) and that 'at the last moment in 1675, he received a government dispensation'; both are given.
MP: the lead says he served 'in 1689–1690 and 1701–1702'; the Later life section says 'in 1689 and 1701'. The role fact follows the lead.
Master of the Mint: the lead says 1699–1727; the text says 'for the last 30 years of his life', which does not fit 1699; the lead's years are used.
The reflecting telescope: 'first known functional reflecting telescope' is the article's wording; 'grinding the mirror himself' rests on 'Newton ground his own mirrors'.
The Leibniz priority question is given as the article gives it (both now credited with independent development; Hall on Newton's nine-year lead).

The 'shoulders of giants' reading: the article says 'some historians argued' it was an oblique attack on Hooke, 'who was presumably short and hunchbacked', and gives a counter-reading from the proverb; Hooke's appearance is left out.
Modern money equivalents (£4.4 million in 2020; nearly £1 billion as a share of GDP; £41,510 saved, roughly £3 million in 2012) are left out.

The article's long list of 'firsts' in the lead (law of cooling, speed of sound, Newtonian fluid, Bézout's theorem, linear regression, and others) and its many rankings and tributes were left out for space and because the guide asks for plain statement; Pope, Lagrange, Einstein and the 1999 polls stand for them.

Left out: the Geographia Generalis editions, the 1699 reflecting quadrant, the 1704 burning mirror, electricity, his views on paper credit, the Newton–Pepys problem, the toad remedy for plague, banknote and statues.
British spelling used; the article's 'recognized' in the state-funeral sentence is written 'recognised'.
